newsitem.title: USA: Democrat loses lead in Georgia Senate race.
newsitem.headline: Democrat loses lead in Georgia Senate race.

text.p: Georgia Democrat Max Cleland has lost his double-digit lead in the U.S. Senate race over Guy Millner and now may be trailing the Republican, according to an opinion poll published Friday.

The survey of 925 likely voters put Cleland and Millner in a statistical dead heat, just a month after the Democrat had held a 16-point lead over his opponent in the race for the Senate seat being vacated by retiring Democrat Sam Nunn.

Overall results put support for Millner at 47 percent, with Cleland's at 45 percent and the number of undecided voters at eight percent. The survey had a three-point margin of error, indicating the two candidates were running about even.
The same poll, conducted Oct. 26-30 by Marketing Workshop Inc. for the Atlanta Journal-Constitution and ABC-affiliate WSB- TV, showed a similar turn in the presidential race in Georgia.

President Clinton had a 15-point lead over Republican challenger Bob Dole a month ago. But the latest results put him only three points ahead, with 43 percent of overall support. Dole's support stood at 40 percent and Texas billionaire Ross Perot's at eight percent.
The Journal-Constitution said Friday's survey concentrated more heavily on voters who were "almost certain" to vote in next Tuesday's election than did the earlier poll.
The survey's results showed Dole and Millner benefiting from a narrowing gender gap, with a larger number of female voters being drawn into the Republican camp.
White voters heavily favoured the Republican candidates, while blacks voiced overwhelming support for Democrats.
The newspaper quoted political experts as saying the racial breakdown was similar to that seen in 1992, when Republican Paul Coverdell defeated Democrat Wyche Fowler for Georgia's other Senate seat.

The tightening of the Senate race appeared to underscore the effectiveness of a negative advertising assault against Cleland, in which Millner has sought to paint him as being soft on crime and an advocate of benefit cuts for the elderly.
The survey showed the Democrat to be plagued by sharply higher negative ratings among women and suburban voters.
